content: 4-Aminobutyrate aminotransferase (ABAT) is a protein encoded by the ABAT gene in humans. This gene is located on chromosome 16 at position 13.2. The ABAT gene is also known by other names, including GABA, GABAT, 4-aminobutyrate transaminase, and NPD009. It is predominantly expressed in neuronal tissues. ABAT belongs to the family of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzymes, which play a significant role in catalyzing reactions involving amino acids. Structurally, ABAT is a homodimer, consisting of two enzyme subunits, each with a molecular weight of approximately 50 kDa. It is estimated that nearly one-third of human synapses utilize gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) as a neurotransmitter. GABA serves various functions in both the central and peripheral nervous systems and is also present in some non-neuronal tissues. The enzymes glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) and GABA aminotransferase (GABA-AT) are critical in regulating GABA concentrations. GABA is a non-fluorescent and non-electroactive molecule, which makes it challenging to study enzymatic reactions involving it, as no peroxidase or dehydrogenase activity has been identified for GABA. One of its notable characteristics is its low lipophilicity, which hinders its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. Researchers have been actively investigating molecules with higher lipophilicity to overcome this limitation. Accurate quantification of GABA concentrations during cellular activity requires high spatial and temporal resolution. Historically, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was used for this purpose. Beyond its role as a neurotransmitter, GABA also functions as a trophic factor, influencing processes such as rapid cell proliferation, cell death, and differentiation. Additionally, GABA plays a role in intracellular communication outside the nervous system. ABAT is responsible for the catabolism of GABA, converting it into succinic semialdehyde. The active form of the enzyme is a homodimer, with each 50-kDa subunit complexed to pyridoxal-5'-phosphate. The protein sequence of ABAT shares over 95% similarity with its pig homolog. In humans, ABAT expression in the liver and brain is regulated by two codominant alleles, with frequencies of 0.56 and 0.44 in Caucasian populations. GABA, as a trophic factor, influences cellular activities such as proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. The ABAT gene directs the production of the GABA-transaminase enzyme, which plays a crucial role in maintaining inhibitory neurotransmission by preventing excessive neuronal activity. ABAT initiates the degradation of GABA, and its suppression can lead to reduced transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation (TLESR) and decreased acid reflux activity. This has implications for the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), as suppressing ABAT's activity may offer therapeutic benefits. ABAT deficiency is a rare genetic disorder. Clinical manifestations of this deficiency have been observed in a Dutch family, two siblings, and a 6-month-old Japanese infant. Common symptoms include hypotonia (low muscle tone, also known as floppy baby syndrome), hyperreflexia (exaggerated reflexes), and developmental delays. The phenotype of ABAT deficiency is characterized by psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, hyperreflexia, lethargy, refractory seizures, and electroencephalogram (EEG) abnormalities. Multiple alternatively spliced transcript variants encoding the same protein isoform have been identified for this gene. Dysfunctional GABA-transaminase activity due to ABAT mutations can result in encephalopathy, particularly in pediatric patients. The life expectancy for individuals with ABAT deficiency is typically less than two years, although some patients have survived beyond this period. Unregulated GABA levels due to ABAT dysfunction can impair growth hormone activity, affecting overall growth. Additionally, reduced GABA concentrations can lead to seizures. Vigabatrin is a pharmacological agent that irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase, leading to increased GABA levels in the brain. This drug has been used to manage conditions associated with low GABA activity. Recent studies have revealed that elevated GABA levels can mitigate the effects of drug addiction. Suppression of ABAT, which increases GABA concentrations, has also been linked to improved outcomes in children with movement disorders. Furthermore, ABAT has been implicated as a genetic factor in GERD. The gene has also been shown to play a role in mitochondrial nucleoside metabolism, underscoring its importance in cellular function.
